records.our_prose: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. If your soil is more acidic than 6.0 or more alkaline than 7.0, lettuce can show yellowing leaves or browning edges even when fertilizer is present. The only way to know your number is to test, so get an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office before adding lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it.

records.our_prose: Interior-valley calendar is heat-inverted with two windows (Table 13.2: August, then November through March). The August window is a short late-summer sowing as peak heat eases; the November-March window is the long mild-winter main season, closing as spring heat returns and drives bolting. records.our_prose: North-coast calendar is cool-limited and summer-inclusive (Table 13.2: February through August), the inverse of the heat-inverted interior and desert. The cool maritime summer is the active growing season, so there is no summer heat pause; the season is bounded instead by the cold, wet winter. Spring sowing begins once soil is workable and warming; the crop runs through summer and closes as winter sets in. In the mildest coastal microclimates, lettuce can be grown nearly year-round with careful variety selection (UC Marin Master Gardeners), but that is a microclimate refinement, not the regional window. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Marin Master Gardeners corroboration for the maritime cool-season pattern.

records.our_prose: South-coast calendar is summer-excluded and winter-dominant (Table 13.2: August through April), a single long mild-season window. It opens as summer heat eases and closes as returning heat drives bolting. The summer gap (roughly May through July) is softer here than in the interior or desert because the maritime-influenced coast stays milder, but it still falls outside the sowing window. Frost is essentially not a limiting factor (South County last frost around mid-February per SLO County MG); heat governs both ends. records.our_prose: In peninsular Florida, lettuce is a cool-season crop, the opposite of up north. Plant from fall through late winter (about September into February), grow it through the mild winter, and skip the summer, when lettuce turns bitter and goes to seed. Winter is your reliable lettuce season here. For the easiest results, aim for the heart of the season, roughly November through January, when temperatures are most consistently cool, rather than the warm edges in early fall or the spring heat ramp.

records.our_prose: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: sow and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and notes that leafy and semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinklers, while heading types are the seasonal, higher-elevation exception. The locally bred 'UH Manoa' (a Green Mignonette selection) and 'Anuenue' are the low-elevation standards; CTAHR describes Manoa as heat-tolerant, slow to bolt, and tip-burn resistant, grown year-round. The hot, long-day months bring a quality dip rather than a production gap: expect faster bolting and more tip-burn, managed with cultivar choice, roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites (per CTAHR shade trials), and a move to higher elevation for head types. Germination falls off above about 81°F, so warm-season sowings benefit from primed seed or a cooler germination spot. Keep soil moisture steady; protect soft-leaved types from heavy rain. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164 (Lettuce Production Guidelines for Hawaii), HGV-2 (Lettuce for the Home Garden), and B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii).

records.our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), lettuce is a spring-and-fall crop built around frost, not heat. Start sowing in spring as soon as the soil warms to about 40°F, usually a few weeks before your last frost, and sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Plant again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. Skip the hottest part of summer, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. For the most reliable results your first season, aim for the spring window from when the soil is workable into early summer, and a fall sowing in July or August depending on your zone, leaving roughly a month before your first frost so young leaves size up while it is still mild. Lettuce takes light frost in stride, so a fall crop can keep going right up to the first hard freeze.

records.our_prose: Region calendar is frost-governed and spring-centric, the standard (non-inverted) lettuce pattern the warm regions invert against. Two succession arms bracket the summer: a spring arm sown from the soil-40°F crossing (a few weeks ahead of last frost) through the bolt-driven close as sustained heat above about 75°F sets in, and a fall arm whose start is heat-floored to roughly July 1 in the coldest zones rather than a flat first-frost-minus-90, since the unclamped offset would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (soil thermoinhibition above about 80°F). The fall arm targets fast-maturing looseleaf at the 30-day baby-leaf end, harvested through light frost rather than to a full head, so the latest viable sow sits about 30 days ahead of first frost with no extra hard margin. Per-arm sowing counts are derived per zone (not a fixed season cap) and range roughly 7 to 10 across zones 3 through 7. Frost is the governing constraint at both ends; summer heat is the interior limit. Spring-sow timing is anchored to MSU (cool-season germination minimum 35 to 40°F) and UMN (direct sow as soil reaches 40°F, 2 to 4 weeks before last frost); the fall arm and heat floor to UMN midsummer-planting guidance and USU (fall lettuce 50 to 75 days before maturity, light frost tolerated to 32°F), with NDSU corroboration for the coldest-zone fall window. In the milder cold zones (6 and 7), a cold frame or row cover extends the harvest several weeks past the outdoor season, with slow winter growth that holds the standing crop rather than expanding it; this is season extension under protection, not part of the default outdoor calendar (VCE and UMN give cold frames and row cover a two-to-four-week spring and fall extension).

records.our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows leaf lettuce on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs March 1 to March 15, the Group B (Semi-Hardy) date for St. George, with leaves ready in about 38 days and the crop cut by late April before it bolts in rising heat. USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table opens the fall lettuce window on June 1, a month earlier than the fall beet and turnip dates, so May is the one genuine bare-ground gap between the spring finish and the fall sowing here. Leaf lettuce tolerates a light frost, per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes, so the fall stand keeps producing well past the November 1 average first frost.

records.source_context: Over-mature greens will be bitter, tough and stringy. It is best to harvest greens in the cool of the morning and process or refrigerate them as soon as possible. Remove any soil from the leaves by running cool water over them.

records.our_prose: Leaf lettuce is one of the quickest and most forgiving crops for a first season. You can be cutting baby leaves in roughly a month from sowing, while a full-sized plant takes longer, about 40 to 80 days depending on the type, with loose-leaf kinds the fastest and heading types the slowest. Because you do not have to wait for a head to form, that early baby-leaf harvest is what makes lettuce feel so fast.

records.source_context: Transplants can be purchased from nurseries and garden centers. Although purchased transplants are more expensive, they are more convenient because you do not have to start your own plants. Home gardeners can also start their own transplants either indoors in flats or other containers, or outdoors in cold frames or hotbeds.
